description: Taking on the Astronaut Health Monitoring Software challenge as a solo project, but always open to good people joining in! Building an interactive health-monitoring platform to help astronauts track vital signs, spot health changes and make informed decisions during long-duration space missions.
summary:
On Mars, a call for help takes 20 minutes to reach Earth, and the reply takes 20 more. Hence, an astronaut who feels unwell must decide alone.
CrewPulse is a prototype health monitor built with Python and Streamlit. It is organised around NASA’s five spaceflight hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields and hostile closed environments. Eleven health readings, including heart rate, temperature, sleep, mood and radiation dose, are checked against sourced ranges and each astronaut’s own baseline. Unusual changes show up early, and combinations such as raised temperature, a faster heart rate and worse sleep are flagged as a possible infection. An interactive dashboard brings it together with a 3D body map, trend charts, daily check-ins and a guide to every reading. Its key feature is mission-aware advice. Near Earth, it says to call the flight surgeon. Far away, it guides the astronaut to act on their own.
CrewPulse is a working prototype that runs on a simulated 180-day mission. With wearables feeding it real readings, it could grow into a tool crews rely on. Our goal is simple: an astronaut who stays safe, even when help is far away.
details:
Who do you call when the nearest doctor is months of travel away, and even a radio message takes 20 minutes to get there?

That is the situation an astronaut on Mars will be in. They live for months in a small spacecraft, with radiation, isolation, low gravity and recycled air all working on the body at once. When something feels wrong, they cannot count on an answer from Earth in time. We built CrewPulse for that moment: a prototype health monitor that helps an astronaut notice a problem early and decide what to do next.

CrewPulse follows 11 daily readings: radiation dose, mood, sleep, social contact, heart rate, blood pressure (high and low), exercise, body temperature, fasting glucose and food intake. We grouped them under NASA's five Human Research Program hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields and hostile closed environments. Every reading has a normal range and a wider watch range taken from medical sources. Resting heart rate, for example, is normal between 60 and 100 beats a minute and on watch between 50 and 110. Each reading shows as green, amber or red, and each hazard takes the status of its worst reading, so the astronaut can see at a glance which risk needs attention.

A range alone does not tell the whole story, because healthy people differ. So CrewPulse learns each astronaut's own baseline from their first 14 days, then warns when a reading drifts away from it, even while it is still inside the normal range. It also tracks weekly trends and looks for combinations of readings. It watches for four patterns: isolation stress, a possible infection, deconditioning risk and a large share of the radiation limit used. A raised temperature with a faster heart rate and worse sleep, for example, points to a possible infection. A readiness score out of 100 gives a quick picture of how the astronaut is doing.

Radiation only builds up, so CrewPulse adds up the daily dose and shows it as a share of NASA's 600 mSv career limit.

Each alert comes with practical advice. If mood and sleep slip, it suggests a fixed sleep window, dimmer lights in the evening and a daily hobby. Because bones and muscles weaken without weight, it reminds the crew to do resistive and treadmill sessions every day.

Our key idea is advice that follows the distance. The user picks where the mission is: the space station, the Moon or Mars. The delay is none on the station, about one second on the Moon and about 20 minutes one way on Mars. Near Earth, CrewPulse tells the astronaut to call the flight surgeon. When the ground is 5 minutes or more away, it switches to autonomous guidance: remeasure, follow the protocol, send a full report and carry on without waiting for a reply. The 5-minute switching point is our own design choice.

CrewPulse has six pages. Mission Control shows readiness, radiation used, the ground reply delay, a card for each hazard, ranked alerts, detected patterns and the recommended next step. Hazards explains each risk, why each reading matters, how to measure it and what to do. Trends charts any reading against its normal range and personal baseline. A rotating 3D body map colours organs by health status and makes the heartbeat at the current heart rate. A daily Check-in lets the astronaut type in readings and sees the results straight away, with streaks, XP and badges to keep routines going in isolation. A Guide explains every reading and lists all 20 sources.

CrewPulse is written in Python, with Streamlit for the interface, pandas for the analysis, plotly for the charts and Three.js for the 3D body. We began with research, reading NASA's Human Research Program pages and radiation protection brief, plus guidance from the CDC, the American Heart Association, Mayo Clinic and MedlinePlus. We ranked 20 sources, putting space agencies and medical bodies above news sites. Every number in the app is tied to a source or labelled as our own design. Then we built a simulated 180-day mission for each location, with an illness written into days 112 to 116 so we could test whether the app catches it. Finally, we ran every page and checked the ranges against their sources.

Therefore, CrewPulse is a web-based software application that runs on simulated missions and manually entered readings, not on real astronaut sensors, and it has not been clinically validated or tested with doctors. It is not a medical device, and its ranges are for healthy adults on Earth.

The same analysis could run on readings from wearables, a blood pressure cuff, a glucose meter and a radiation dosimeter. Clinicians would test and refine the advice, and ranges built for space would replace the Earth ones. Our aim is an astronaut who can spot a health problem early and make a good decision, even when help is far away.
